home.eyebrow: A practice shaped by the mountains
home.intro: Mountaineering is the pursuit of travel through mountain terrain, from long high-altitude treks to technical rock, snow and ice climbing. It combines physical preparation, sound judgment, practical skills and respect for changing conditions.
home.mission: Alpine Ascents creates safe, challenging and fun expeditions. We pair careful planning and experienced leaders with the joy of moving through wild places, helping each climber return stronger and with a story worth sharing.

history.title: A brief history of mountaineering
history.summary: From early summit journeys to modern alpine craft, mountaineering has always mixed curiosity with preparation.

sections.title: Curiosity becomes a pursuit
sections.text: For centuries, mountains were crossed for trade, work and survival. By the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, exploration and scientific observation brought new attention to high peaks, and organized climbing began to take shape.

sections.title: Skills and equipment evolve
sections.text: Better maps, weather knowledge, ropes, boots and protective equipment changed what climbers could attempt. Local expertise remained essential, and the strongest expeditions learned to value it.

sections.title: A living tradition
sections.text: Today's mountaineering includes many styles and communities. Its lasting lessons are careful preparation, humility in changing conditions and responsibility for the people and places along the way.

types.title: Types of mountaineering
types.summary: Different objectives call for different skills, equipment and levels of commitment.
types.alt: High summit under a night sky

sections.title: Trekking and hill walking
sections.text: Non-technical routes focus on navigation, endurance and adapting to terrain. Multi-day treks add campcraft, load management and thoughtful pacing.

sections.title: Alpine and glacier climbing
sections.text: Alpine routes may combine rock, snow and ice. Climbers need efficient movement, rope systems, glacier awareness and the ability to make decisions as conditions change.

sections.title: Rock and expedition climbing
sections.text: Rock objectives emphasize movement and protection on steep ground. Long expeditions add remote logistics, acclimatization, teamwork and a wider margin for uncertainty.

techniques.title: Mountain techniques
techniques.summary: Good technique is deliberate, practiced and matched to the terrain and the team's ability.

sections.title: Movement and pacing
sections.text: Use a steady pace that allows conversation, place each step with care and pause before fatigue undermines judgment. On steep terrain, keep three points of contact whenever appropriate.

sections.title: Rope and protection
sections.text: Rope systems, knots, anchors and protective gear require hands-on instruction and regular practice. Choose systems for the actual terrain and team, and check one another before committing.

sections.title: Navigation and decisions
sections.text: Plan with maps and reliable forecasts, identify landmarks and escape options, and reassess at every transition. Turn around when conditions or the team's margin deteriorates.

sheltering.title: Sheltering in the mountains
sheltering.summary: A warm, dry and well-chosen shelter supports recovery and safer decisions.
sheltering.alt: Mountain tent at an alpine campsite

sections.title: Choose a protected site
sections.text: Avoid avalanche paths, rockfall zones, exposed ridgelines, dry streambeds and fragile vegetation. Check local guidance and choose terrain with safe access and drainage.

sections.title: Plan for conditions
sections.text: Match your shelter and sleep system to expected wind, precipitation and temperatures, with a buffer for forecast changes. Keep essential insulation and emergency equipment accessible.

sections.title: Leave camp well
sections.text: Use established sites where possible, store food responsibly, pack out all waste and leave natural objects undisturbed. Follow local fire and sanitation rules.

hazards.title: Recognizing mountain hazards
hazards.summary: Risk changes with weather, terrain, altitude and the condition of every person in the group.
hazards.alt: Storm clouds around a mountain ridge

sections.title: Weather and exposure
sections.text: Wind, lightning, whiteout, cold and rapid temperature changes can turn manageable terrain serious. Review forecasts and identify sheltered alternatives before setting out.

sections.title: Terrain and snow
sections.text: Rockfall, avalanches, crevasses, loose ground and water crossings require specific training and local information. Avoid terrain beyond your team's competence and current conditions.

sections.title: Altitude and health
sections.text: Acclimatize gradually, stay hydrated and watch for headache, nausea, unusual fatigue or confusion. Worsening symptoms require stopping ascent and descending; severe symptoms need urgent help.

records.title: Mountain records and landmarks
records.summary: A few remarkable elevations put the scale and variety of the world's ranges into perspective.
records.alt: Mountain peaks above a high alpine lake

sections.title: Everest · 8,848.86 m
sections.text: Mount Everest is the highest elevation on Earth, on the Nepal-China border. Its altitude and conditions demand extensive preparation.

sections.title: K2 · 8,611 m
sections.text: The world's second-highest mountain has a remote setting and demanding terrain, making it a serious expedition objective.

sections.title: Aconcagua · about 6,961 m
sections.text: Aconcagua in Argentina is the highest mountain outside Asia. High altitude makes acclimatization important even on its non-technical normal route.

clubs.title: Find your mountain community
clubs.summary: Clubs and local groups make it easier to learn, meet partners and build experience gradually.
clubs.alt: Group of hikers following a mountain trail

sections.title: Learn with others
sections.text: Look for established clubs that offer qualified instruction, beginner-friendly outings and clear safety practices. Ask how leaders assess conditions and support different experience levels.

sections.title: Build experience steadily
sections.text: Start with achievable objectives, practice navigation and outdoor skills, and keep a record of your outings. Reliable partners communicate openly about goals and limits.

sections.title: Take part locally
sections.text: Search for mountaineering associations, climbing gyms, outdoor education programs and conservation groups in your region. Confirm current details directly with each organization.

gallery.title: Mountain gallery
gallery.summary: A glimpse of the landscapes, weather and small moments that make time in the mountains memorable.

sections.title: High places, quiet moments
sections.text: The mountain experience is more than a summit: changing light, a shared meal and the rhythm of a long trail are part of the journey.

sections.title: Travel thoughtfully
sections.text: Photograph responsibly, give wildlife and other visitors space, and avoid geotagging sensitive locations where extra attention could cause harm.

latest.summary: Conditions and access change quickly. Treat these notes as a starting point, not a substitute for local, current information.

sections.title: Check before you go
sections.text: Review official forecasts, park and land-manager notices, avalanche bulletins and route reports close to your departure date.

sections.title: Share a trip plan
sections.text: Leave a trusted contact your route, expected return time and the action to take if you are overdue. Update them when plans change.
